batch: Wave 3 - Deep Security, Scalability, Storage & Protocol Invariants

issues.title: nft-marketplace: Replace vulnerable push-based bid refunds with pull-based claims to prevent auction-locking DoS
issues.body:
In `contracts/nft-marketplace/src/lib.rs` (lines 1027–1032), `place_bid` executes an immediate inline token transfer to refund the previous highest bidder:

```rust
// Refund previous bidder
if auction.current_bid > 0 {
    let prev = auction.current_bidder.clone();
    let pc = token::Client::new(&env, &auction.currency);
    pc.transfer(&env.current_contract_address(), &prev, &auction.current_bid);
}
```

## Why this matters

This is a classic "push over pull" smart contract vulnerability. If `prev` is a contract address whose fallback or receive method fails, or an account with a revoked/frozen trustline, the token transfer will panic and revert the entire transaction. A malicious actor can place a bid from such an account, permanently preventing any subsequent higher bids from executing. The attacker wins the auction at an artificially low price because all competing bids are locked out.

## Tasks

- [ ] Remove inline `token::Client::transfer` refund from `place_bid`
- [ ] Implement pull-based pending refund storage: `DataKey::PendingRefund(Address, Address) -> i128` (keyed by `(bidder, token_address)`)
- [ ] In `place_bid`, credit the outbid user's pending refund balance in storage: `pending_refunds.add(prev, auction.current_bid)`
- [ ] Implement public entry point: `pub fn claim_bid_refund(env: Env, bidder: Address, token: Address) -> Result<i128, MarketError>` allowing users to withdraw accumulated refunds safely
- [ ] Emit an event `emit_bid_refund_credited` and `emit_bid_refund_claimed`
- [ ] Add unit tests in `contracts/nft-marketplace/src/lib.rs` simulating failing refund recipients and verifying that subsequent valid bids succeed

## Files to look at

- `contracts/nft-marketplace/src/lib.rs`
- `contracts/nft-marketplace/src/storage.rs`

## Acceptance criteria

- `place_bid` never transfers tokens to external third parties during bid placement
- Outbid users can claim their refund balances asynchronously via `claim_bid_refund`
- Auctions cannot be locked or griefed by uncooperative or reverting previous bidders

---
**Skills:** Rust, Soroban Token SDK, DeFi Security  
**Estimated effort:** 1–2 days

issues.title: nft-marketplace: Eliminate monolithic `KEY_COLLECTIONS` map in instance storage to prevent 64KB quota exhaustion
issues.body:
In `contracts/nft-marketplace/src/lib.rs` (lines 375–403), `update_collection_stats` and `collection_exists` manage collections via a single monolithic `Map<Address, CollectionInfo>` stored in instance storage under `KEY_COLLECTIONS`:

```rust
fn update_collection_stats(
    env: &Env,
    collection: &Address,
    listing_delta: i32,
    auction_delta: i32,
) {
    let collections: Map<Address, CollectionInfo> =
        instance_get(env, &KEY_COLLECTIONS).unwrap_or_else(|| Map::new(env));
    if let Some(mut info) = collections.get(collection.clone()) {
        ...
        collections.set(collection.clone(), info);
        instance_set(env, &KEY_COLLECTIONS, &collections);
    }
}
```

## Why this matters

Soroban instance storage has a hard ceiling of 64 KB across all entries. Every time any listing or auction is created, filled, or cancelled across the entire marketplace, `KEY_COLLECTIONS` is fully deserialized from instance storage, modified, and reserialized. As the number of registered NFT collections grows, this single map will exceed the 64 KB instance storage limit, causing all marketplace activities to panic and bricking the contract.

## Tasks

- [ ] Replace `KEY_COLLECTIONS` monolithic map with individual persistent storage keys: `DataKey::CollectionInfo(Address)`
- [ ] Update `register_collection`, `get_collection`, and `collection_exists` to use direct `O(1)` persistent storage lookups
- [ ] Update `update_collection_stats` to mutate only the specific collection's storage entry
- [ ] Ensure persistent collection entries use TTL bump helpers (`shared::storage::persistent_set`)
- [ ] Add a stress test registering 100+ collections and verifying zero instance storage bloat

## Files to look at

- `contracts/nft-marketplace/src/lib.rs`
- `shared/src/storage.rs`

## Acceptance criteria

- Collection metadata and stats are stored under individual persistent keys
- `update_collection_stats` operates in `O(1)` time and storage footprint
- The marketplace supports an arbitrary number of collections without exhausting instance storage

---
**Skills:** Rust, Soroban Storage Architecture  
**Estimated effort:** 1 day

issues.title: rebalancer: Fix precision loss and unchecked arithmetic in fee calculator
issues.body:
In `contracts/rebalancer-contract/src/fee_calculator.rs` (lines 4–11):

```rust
pub fn calculate_total_fees(trades: &Vec<Trade>) -> u128 {
    let mut total_fees = 0;
    for trade in trades.iter() {
        // Placeholder fee calculation (0.1% of trade amount)
        total_fees += trade.amount / 1000;
    }
    total_fees
}
```

And in `contracts/rebalancer-contract/src/strategy_executor.rs` (line 58):
```rust
let fee = trade.amount / 1000;
total_fees = total_fees.saturating_add(fee);
```

## Why this matters

1. **Precision Loss:** The integer division `trade.amount / 1000` truncates any trade amount under 1,000 stroops (sub-cent values) directly to zero fees. A 0.1% fee should be represented in basis points (10 BPS) with round-up handling to avoid dust leakage.
2. **Unchecked Arithmetic:** `total_fees += trade.amount / 1000` in `fee_calculator.rs` uses unchecked addition `+=` rather than `checked_add` or `saturating_add`, which can panic on high-volume batches.
3. **Hardcoded Fee Rate:** The 0.1% fee is hardcoded in two separate files rather than queried from governance or pool configurations.

## Tasks

- [ ] Standardize fee calculation using basis points (`shared::math::bps_of` or equivalent with ceil rounding for dust)
- [ ] Replace unchecked addition `+=` with `checked_add` returning `Result<u128, Error>` or `saturating_add`
- [ ] Query fee basis points from contract configuration rather than hardcoding `1000`
- [ ] Ensure `strategy_executor.rs` calls `fee_calculator.rs` rather than duplicating the calculation
- [ ] Add unit tests in `contracts/rebalancer-contract/src/tests.rs` for amounts < 1000, boundary values (`u128::MAX`), and varied BPS tiers

## Files to look at

- `contracts/rebalancer-contract/src/fee_calculator.rs`
- `contracts/rebalancer-contract/src/strategy_executor.rs`
- `shared/src/math.rs`

## Acceptance criteria

- Fee calculation is accurate to fractional units without zero-truncation leakage
- Fee summation is strictly overflow-safe
- Single unified fee calculation logic shared across all rebalancer modules

---
**Skills:** Rust, Financial Mathematics, Soroban  
**Estimated effort:** 1 day

issues.title: rebalancer: Replace hardcoded trade capacity limit with dynamic liquidity pool depth queries
issues.body:
In `contracts/rebalancer-contract/src/strategy_executor.rs` (lines 46–56) and `contracts/rebalancer-contract/src/lib.rs` (line 96), trade validation enforces a static trade capacity limit:

```rust
if trade.amount > 10_000_000_000 {
    trades_failed += 1;
    trade_statuses.push_back(TradeReceipt {
        asset_pair: trade.asset_pair.clone(),
        amount: trade.amount,
        status: TradeStatus::Failed,
        fee: 0,
        error_code: Some(ERROR_EXCEEDS_CAPACITY),
    });
    continue;
}
```

## Why this matters

The threshold `10_000_000_000` (which corresponds to 1,000 units in standard 7-decimal tokens) is an arbitrary hardcoded integer. This creates two critical issues:
1. For deep, highly liquid pools (e.g. XLM/USDC with millions in reserves), valid institutional or NGO portfolio rebalancing trades are arbitrarily rejected.
2. For thin, illiquid pools, `10_000_000_000` is dangerously high and could drain substantial pool reserves, causing extreme price slippage.

## Tasks

- [ ] Remove the hardcoded `10_000_000_000` trade capacity limit
- [ ] Implement configurable capacity parameters per asset pair stored in contract storage
- [ ] Query liquidity pool reserves or evaluate expected price impact via `slippage_predictor` before accepting trade size
- [ ] Allow governance or contract managers to adjust maximum trade size per pair via administrative entry points
- [ ] Update unit tests in `contracts/rebalancer-contract/src/tests.rs` to verify dynamic capacity enforcement

## Files to look at

- `contracts/rebalancer-contract/src/strategy_executor.rs`
- `contracts/rebalancer-contract/src/lib.rs`
- `contracts/rebalancer-contract/src/slippage_predictor.rs`

## Acceptance criteria

- Rebalancer trade capacity is determined dynamically per asset pair and pool depth
- High-liquidity trades are no longer falsely rejected by an arbitrary static ceiling
- Low-liquidity trades are safeguarded against excessive price impact

---
**Skills:** Rust, DeFi Liquidity Management  
**Estimated effort:** 2–3 days

issues.title: aid-contract: Implement batch aid allocation (`batch_create_aid`) for NGO operations
issues.body:
In `contracts/aid-contract/src/lib.rs` (lines 190–280), `AidContract` only allows creating aid records one by one via `create_aid`:

```rust
pub fn create_aid(
    env: Env,
    donor: Address,
    recipient: Address,
    token: Address,
    amount: i128,
    purpose: Symbol,
    expiry_ledger: u32,
) -> Result<u64, AidError>
```

## Why this matters

Humanitarian aid organizations (e.g. UN agencies, Red Cross, disaster relief NGOs) routinely disburse assistance to dozens or hundreds of beneficiaries simultaneously. Sending a separate on-chain transaction for every beneficiary creates severe operational bottlenecks: sequence number collisions, high aggregate base fees, and partial deployment failures. A single batch transaction dramatically reduces overhead and guarantees atomic distribution.

## Tasks

- [ ] Define `BatchAidAllocation` struct: `recipient: Address`, `amount: i128`, `purpose: Symbol`, `expiry_ledger: u32`
- [ ] Implement `pub fn batch_create_aid(env: Env, donor: Address, token: Address, allocations: Vec<BatchAidAllocation>) -> Result<Vec<u64>, AidError>`
- [ ] Enforce an upper bound on batch size (e.g. `MAX_BATCH_SIZE = 50`) to remain well within Soroban CPU and footprint budgets
- [ ] Execute a single consolidated `token::Client::transfer` from `donor` to the contract for `sum(amounts)`
- [ ] Assign sequential IDs and populate individual records with shared token configuration
- [ ] Add unit and fuzz tests in `contracts/aid-contract/src/tests.rs` verifying atomicity and rollback on invalid entries

## Files to look at

- `contracts/aid-contract/src/lib.rs`
- `contracts/aid-contract/src/storage.rs`
- `contracts/aid-contract/src/tests.rs`

## Acceptance criteria

- NGOs can disburse aid to up to 50 recipients in a single atomic transaction
- Token transfers are consolidated into a single transfer call, minimizing ledger overhead
- If any entry in the batch fails validation, the entire batch reverts

---
**Skills:** Rust, Soroban Token SDK, API Design  
**Estimated effort:** 2 days

issues.title: aid-contract: Replace unbounded linear vectors in `SearchIndex`, `DonorAids`, and `RecipientIndex` with paginated bucketing
issues.body:
In `contracts/aid-contract/src/storage.rs` (lines 140–184), `append_donor_aid`, `append_recipient_aid`, and `set_search_index` append aid IDs to unbounded `Vec<u64>` structures stored under single persistent keys:

```rust
let mut ids = get_donor_aids(env, donor);
ids.push_back(aid_id);
persistent_set(env, &DataKey::DonorAids(donor.clone()), &ids);
```

And for `SearchIndex`:
```rust
pub fn get_search_index(env: &Env) -> Vec<u64> {
    persistent_get(env, &DataKey::SearchIndex).unwrap_or_else(|| Vec::new(env))
}
pub fn set_search_index(env: &Env, ids: &Vec<u64>) {
    persistent_set(env, &DataKey::SearchIndex, ids);
}
```

## Why this matters

Every time an aid is created, the contract loads the full `Vec<u64>`, appends an element, and writes it back. As soon as an active donor creates several hundred aids or total aids across the protocol grow, this vector exceeds the 64 KB storage entry limit and CPU limits, causing all new aid creation to fail permanently with storage write errors.

## Tasks

- [ ] Replace monolithic vectors with chunked/bucketed storage keys: `DataKey::DonorAidsPage(Address, u32)` with a bounded page size (e.g. 50 IDs per page)
- [ ] Replace `DataKey::RecipientIndex(Address)` with bucketed pages: `DataKey::RecipientAidsPage(Address, u32)`
- [ ] Replace `DataKey::SearchIndex` flat vector with a cursor-based sequence index or bounded recent-items window
- [ ] Track count metadata per donor/recipient in `DataKey::DonorAidCount(donor)` to allow `O(1)` append operations
- [ ] Update `list_aids_by_donor` and `list_aids_by_recipient` to query page buckets directly
- [ ] Add stress tests in `contracts/aid-contract/src/tests.rs` simulating hundreds of aid creations without storage degradation

## Files to look at

- `contracts/aid-contract/src/storage.rs`
- `contracts/aid-contract/src/lib.rs`
- `contracts/aid-contract/src/types.rs`

## Acceptance criteria

- Storage write cost for aid creation is `O(1)` regardless of historical volume
- No single persistent storage entry grows unbounded
- Paginated queries operate cleanly across page boundaries

---
**Skills:** Rust, Soroban Storage Optimization  
**Estimated effort:** 2–3 days

issues.title: aid-contract: Support milestone-based phased aid disbursements and tranche releases
issues.body:
In `contracts/aid-contract/src/lib.rs` (lines 310–355), `claim_aid` operates as an all-or-nothing payout:

```rust
pub fn claim_aid(env: Env, recipient: Address, aid_id: u64) -> Result<(), AidError>
```

Once claimed, 100% of the allocated amount is transferred, and the aid record transitions permanently to `AidStatus::Claimed`.

## Why this matters

Many humanitarian relief and development programs (such as infrastructure rebuilding, seasonal agricultural assistance, or ongoing medical treatment) require phased milestone disbursements. Releasing full funding upfront creates severe moral hazard and risk of fund diversion. Support for milestone tranches allows donors to fund long-term initiatives where funds are released incrementally upon verification of progress.

## Tasks

- [ ] Define `AidMilestone` struct: `description: Symbol`, `amount: i128`, `verified: bool`, `claimed: bool`
- [ ] Extend `AidRecord` or add persistent storage key `DataKey::Milestones(u64) -> Vec<AidMilestone>`
- [ ] Implement `pub fn claim_aid_milestone(env: Env, recipient: Address, aid_id: u64, milestone_index: u32) -> Result<(), AidError>`
- [ ] Implement `pub fn verify_milestone(env: Env, caller: Address, aid_id: u64, milestone_index: u32) -> Result<(), AidError>` restricted to authorized inspectors or oracle submitters
- [ ] Allow donors to refund remaining unclaimed/unverified tranches after expiration
- [ ] Add unit tests verifying multi-tranche disbursements, verification requirements, and partial refund handling

## Files to look at

- `contracts/aid-contract/src/lib.rs`
- `contracts/aid-contract/src/types.rs`
- `contracts/aid-contract/src/storage.rs`
- `contracts/aid-contract/src/tests.rs`

## Acceptance criteria

- Donors can configure single-payout or milestone-based aid programs
- Beneficiaries can only claim tranches that have been verified by authorized entities
- Unclaimed or unverified milestone funds are safely refundable to the donor upon expiry

---
**Skills:** Rust, Smart Contract Design, Humanitarian Workflows  
**Estimated effort:** 3–4 days

issues.title: oracle: Implement staking and slashing mechanism for price feed submitters
issues.body:
In `contracts/oracle-contract/src/lib.rs` (lines 70–130), `register_submitter` allows an admin to authorize submitters, who can then submit price feeds with zero economic stake:

```rust
pub fn submit_price(
    env: Env,
    submitter: Address,
    feed_id: Symbol,
    price: i128,
    decimals: u32,
    timestamp: u64,
    nonce: u64,
) -> Result<u64, OracleError>
```

## Why this matters

Price feeds directly determine rebalancer trade execution and aid currency valuations. If a submitter key is compromised or acts maliciously by submitting off-market prices, the only available recourse is retrospective admin deactivation via `deactivate_submitter`. There is no economic bonding, slashing mechanism, or financial penalty to disincentivize fraudulent or negligent submissions.

## Tasks

- [ ] Require submitters to deposit a minimum stake of protocol collateral (e.g. XLM or USDC) upon registration
- [ ] Store submitter stake amounts under `DataKey::SubmitterStake(Address)`
- [ ] Implement `slash_submitter(env: Env, caller: Address, submitter: Address, penalty_amount: i128, reason: Symbol)` executable by governance
- [ ] Direct slashed collateral to the `TreasuryContract` reserve
- [ ] Implement `unstake(env: Env, submitter: Address)` subject to an unbonding cooldown window
- [ ] Add unit tests in `contracts/oracle-contract/src/tests.rs` verifying staking enforcement, slashing execution, and unbonding locks

## Files to look at

- `contracts/oracle-contract/src/lib.rs`
- `contracts/oracle-contract/src/storage.rs`
- `contracts/oracle-contract/src/errors.rs`
- `contracts/treasury-contract/src/lib.rs`

## Acceptance criteria

- Submitter addresses cannot submit prices without maintaining active staked collateral
- Malicious or aberrant submitters can be slashed by governance
- Unstaking enforces an unbonding cooldown to prevent immediate exit after posting bad data

---
**Skills:** Rust, Crypto-economics, Oracle Security  
**Estimated effort:** 3 days

issues.title: oracle: Replace hardcoded `MIN_PRICE_QUORUM = 2` with governance-configurable quorum parameters
issues.body:
In `contracts/oracle-contract/src/lib.rs` (line 44), the minimum price quorum is defined as a fixed compile-time constant:

```rust
const MIN_PRICE_QUORUM: u32 = 2;
```

This constant is checked during price retrieval and medianization.

## Why this matters

As the protocol scales from initial testnet deployment to production, the required number of independent oracle submitters needs to increase (e.g. requiring at least 5 out of 7 signers on high-value asset pairs). Hardcoding this value in bytecode prevents governance from adjusting quorum requirements without recompiling and executing a complete contract code upgrade.

## Tasks

- [ ] Store quorum configuration in instance storage: `DataKey::MinPriceQuorum` and optional per-feed overrides `DataKey::FeedQuorum(Symbol)`
- [ ] Implement `set_min_quorum(env: Env, caller: Address, min_quorum: u32) -> Result<(), OracleError>` restricted to admin/governance
- [ ] Update `get_latest_price` and median aggregation to check against dynamically configured quorum
- [ ] Validate that `min_quorum >= 1` and cannot exceed total active submitters
- [ ] Add unit tests verifying runtime updates to quorum thresholds and feed validation

## Files to look at

- `contracts/oracle-contract/src/lib.rs`
- `contracts/oracle-contract/src/storage.rs`
- `contracts/oracle-contract/src/tests.rs`

## Acceptance criteria

- Oracle quorum threshold can be modified dynamically via authorized governance calls
- Feeds fail if active submitter count falls below the configured quorum
- Zero-code-upgrade parameter flexibility for production mainnet tuning

---
**Skills:** Rust, Oracle Design, Governance  
**Estimated effort:** 1 day

issues.title: treasury: Implement rolling-window velocity limits and circuit breaker on cumulative outflows
issues.body:
In `contracts/treasury-contract/src/lib.rs` (lines 359–364), `withdraw` enforces a per-transaction limit:

```rust
let limit: i128 = instance_get(&env, &MAX_WD).unwrap_or(0);
if amount > limit {
    return Err(Error::WithdrawalLimitExceeded);
}
```

However, there is no cumulative velocity limit over a rolling time window (e.g., maximum 100,000 tokens per 24 hours).

## Why this matters

A compromised manager account or exploited cross-contract caller can simply call `withdraw(MAX_WD)` repeatedly in rapid succession (even within the same ledger block), bypassing the intent of the withdrawal limit and draining the entire treasury reserve within minutes.

## Tasks

- [ ] Define rolling window parameters in storage: `window_size_seconds: u64` (e.g. 86,400s) and `max_window_outflow: i128`
- [ ] Track rolling window outflow state: `(current_window_start: u64, cumulative_outflow: i128)` per token asset
- [ ] In `withdraw` and `distribute_reward`, compute whether the current timestamp exceeds the window start; if so, roll over; otherwise, assert `cumulative_outflow + amount <= max_window_outflow`
- [ ] Implement an automated circuit breaker that pauses withdrawals and emits a high-priority alert if velocity limits are breached
- [ ] Add unit tests in `contracts/treasury-contract/src/test.rs` asserting rapid successive withdrawals trigger velocity rejections

## Files to look at

- `contracts/treasury-contract/src/lib.rs`
- `contracts/treasury-contract/src/test.rs`
- `shared/src/timeline.rs`

## Acceptance criteria

- Treasury rejects outflows that exceed cumulative velocity quotas over rolling time horizons
- Velocity tracking is partitioned cleanly per token asset
- Automated circuit breaker protects treasury from rapid drain exploits

---
**Skills:** Rust, Financial Risk Management, Smart Contract Security  
**Estimated effort:** 2–3 days

issues.title: treasury: Implement idle reserve allocation to Stellar DEX / AMM liquidity pools (SEP-41)
issues.body:
In `contracts/treasury-contract/src/lib.rs`, treasury reserves sit entirely idle in the contract's instance balance, earning zero yield and providing no protocol utility.

## Why this matters

Humanitarian aid treasuries often hold millions of dollars in reserves waiting for disbursement during future emergency crises. On Stellar, Soroban contracts can interact with native Stellar Liquidity Pools and SEP-41 token interfaces to deploy a portion of idle capital (e.g. a conservative 20–30% reserve buffer) into stable liquidity pools or yield vaults, generating organic returns for the humanitarian aid endowment.

## Tasks

- [ ] Define `ReserveStrategy` interface supporting `deposit_reserve`, `withdraw_reserve`, and `harvest_yield`
- [ ] Implement configurable allocation caps (e.g. maximum 30% of category balance can be committed to yield strategies)
- [ ] Ensure instant liquidity recall: when aid disbursements or emergency withdrawals occur, auto-unwind positions if liquid cash is insufficient
- [ ] Add administrative entry points for governance to approve or revoke yield strategy adapters
- [ ] Add integration tests verifying safe allocation, withdrawal, and yield recording

## Files to look at

- `contracts/treasury-contract/src/lib.rs`
- `contracts/treasury-contract/src/test.rs`

## Acceptance criteria

- Treasury can allocate idle funds to verified Stellar liquidity pools up to configured safety limits
- Principal reserves remain fully protected and recallable on demand
- Yield earned is recorded in treasury accounting under a designated revenue category

---
**Skills:** Rust, Soroban SEP-41, DeFi Yield Strategies  
**Estimated effort:** 3–5 days

issues.title: governance: Add dynamic percentage quorum requirements for multi-sig proposals
issues.body:
In `contracts/governance-contract/src/lib.rs` (lines 399–402), proposal execution relies solely on a fixed integer threshold:

```rust
let threshold: u32 = instance_get(&env, &KEY_THRESHOLD).unwrap_or(0);
if proposal.approval_count < threshold {
    return Err(Error::BelowThreshold);
}
```

## Why this matters

If the administrative team expands from 3 to 10 signers, the threshold remains fixed at its initial number (e.g. 2) unless manually adjusted. A static threshold fails to enforce genuine super-majority consensus as member counts fluctuate, allowing a small minority to execute high-impact proposals without quorum.

## Tasks

- [ ] Store total active admin count alongside membership
- [ ] Add configurable quorum percentage basis points: `quorum_bps: u32` (e.g., 6,000 BPS = 60% quorum)
- [ ] In `execute`, calculate `required_approvals = max(threshold, ceil(active_admins * quorum_bps / 10_000))`
- [ ] Reject proposal execution if `proposal.approval_count < required_approvals`
- [ ] Add unit tests verifying dynamic threshold escalation when new admins are added or removed

## Files to look at

- `contracts/governance-contract/src/lib.rs`

## Acceptance criteria

- Proposal execution mandates both a minimum numerical threshold AND a dynamic percentage quorum of active admins
- Quorum recalculates dynamically based on live admin registry size
- Multi-sig security scales safely with organizational expansion

---
**Skills:** Rust, Governance Design, Multi-sig Security  
**Estimated effort:** 1–2 days

issues.title: governance: Support atomic batch proposal action execution (`batch_execute_actions`)
issues.body:
In `contracts/governance-contract/src/lib.rs` (lines 125–135), the `Proposal` struct only supports a single `action: ProposalAction`:

```rust
pub struct Proposal {
    pub id: u64,
    pub proposer: Address,
    pub action: ProposalAction,
    ...
}
```

## Why this matters

Complex administrative operations—such as rotating multi-contract keys, updating fee tiers simultaneously with withdrawal caps, or executing an upgrade across multiple interdependent contracts—require multiple distinct actions. If executed via separate proposals, intermediate partial-execution states can break protocol consistency or expose vulnerabilities.

## Tasks

- [ ] Extend proposal data structures to support `Batch(Vec<ProposalAction>)` in `ProposalAction`
- [ ] Implement atomic execution loop in `execute_action`: iterate through all actions and execute each sequentially within the transaction
- [ ] Ensure that if any action in the batch fails, the entire transaction reverts atomically
- [ ] Enforce maximum batch size (e.g. 10 actions) to avoid transaction CPU exhaustion
- [ ] Add tests in `contracts/governance-contract/src/lib.rs` verifying atomic multi-action proposals and rollback on partial failure

## Files to look at

- `contracts/governance-contract/src/lib.rs`

## Acceptance criteria

- Governance can bundle multiple parameter changes, role updates, and contract upgrades into a single proposal
- All actions execute in an all-or-nothing atomic transaction
- Protocol state is never left in a partially applied configuration

---
**Skills:** Rust, Soroban Governance, Atomic Execution  
**Estimated effort:** 2 days

issues.title: referral: Add human-readable vanity referral codes mapped to Stellar addresses
issues.body:
In `contracts/referral-contract/src/lib.rs` (lines 320–350), `register` requires callers to provide the direct 56-character Stellar public address of their referrer:

```rust
pub fn register(env: Env, wallet: Address, referrer: Address) -> Result<(), Error>
```

## Why this matters

In humanitarian campaigns and charity drives, donors and advocates share branded campaign codes (e.g. `SAVE-THE-CHILDREN`, `ALICE2026`, `WATER-FOR-ALL`) on social media, QR codes, and physical flyers. Forcing users to enter raw cryptographic addresses hinders adoption and leads to typographical errors.

## Tasks

- [ ] Add storage mapping for vanity codes: `DataKey::ReferralCode(Symbol) -> Address` and `DataKey::AddressToCode(Address) -> Symbol`
- [ ] Implement `register_referral_code(env: Env, owner: Address, code: Symbol) -> Result<(), Error>` validating format (alphanumeric, 3–16 characters) and uniqueness
- [ ] Implement `register_by_code(env: Env, wallet: Address, code: Symbol) -> Result<(), Error>` that resolves the code to the referrer address
- [ ] Implement reverse lookup query `get_code_by_address(env: Env, address: Address) -> Option<Symbol>`
- [ ] Add comprehensive unit tests in `contracts/referral-contract/src/lib.rs` covering vanity registration, resolution, duplicates, and cycle prevention

## Files to look at

- `contracts/referral-contract/src/lib.rs`

## Acceptance criteria

- Users can claim unique alphanumeric vanity referral codes
- New wallets can join the referral graph using either a raw address or vanity code
- Vanity codes resolve deterministically and prevent collisions or squatting

**Estimated effort:** 1–2 days

issues.title: payments: Add multi-stage milestone escrow releases and partial dispute arbitration
issues.body:
In `contracts/payments-contract/src/lib.rs` (lines 307–350), the escrow system only supports binary outcomes: releasing 100% of funds to the beneficiary (`release_escrow_entry`), or refunding 100% to the depositor (`refund_escrow_entry`).

## Why this matters

For humanitarian contractor engagements, goods procurement, and logistics shipping, payments need to support milestone tranches (e.g. 20% deposit, 40% on dispatch, 40% on receipt) and partial arbitration splits if a dispute arises. Forcing an all-or-nothing settlement either unjustly penalizes contractors or endangers donor funds.

## Tasks

- [ ] Extend `EscrowRecord` to track `milestones: Vec<Milestone>` or `released_amount: i128`
- [ ] Implement `release_milestone(env: Env, caller: Address, escrow_id: u64, amount: i128) -> Result<(), Error>`
- [ ] Implement `resolve_dispute(env: Env, caller: Address, escrow_id: u64, beneficiary_amount: i128, refund_amount: i128) -> Result<(), Error>` executable by authorized arbiters
- [ ] Ensure total released + refunded amounts strictly equal the original deposited escrow amount
- [ ] Add unit tests in `contracts/payments-contract/src/test.rs` verifying partial payouts, dispute settlements, and invariant conservation

## Files to look at

- `contracts/payments-contract/src/lib.rs`
- `contracts/payments-contract/src/test.rs`

## Acceptance criteria

- Escrow deposits can be released incrementally across multiple milestones
- Arbitrators can divide escrowed funds between depositor and beneficiary in case of dispute
- Value conservation invariant (`released + refunded + remaining == total`) is strictly maintained

---
**Skills:** Rust, Escrow Protocols, Arbitration Mechanisms  
**Estimated effort:** 2–3 days

issues.title: upgradeability: Add automated state snapshotting and post-migration rollback validation hook
issues.body:
In `contracts/upgradeability/src/lib.rs` (lines 15–23), contract upgrades call `env.deployer().update_current_contract_wasm()` and invoke migration hooks. However, there is no built-in pre-migration state snapshot or post-migration rollback safety mechanism.

## Why this matters

If a migration hook introduces data corruption, violates a core financial invariant, or panics midway through a multi-step migration, the contract bytecode has already been upgraded, leaving the protocol bricked with no automated recovery path.

## Tasks

- [ ] Define `PostUpgradeValidation` interface requiring a target contract to run sanity checks on its internal state after migration
- [ ] Record pre-upgrade state metadata (e.g., previous WASM hash, critical account balance roots) in `UpgradeabilityContract`
- [ ] Execute post-upgrade validation hook within the upgrade transaction; if validation returns an error, execute an immediate rollback of the WASM bytecode to the previous hash
- [ ] Emit detailed audit events recording validation metrics and rollback triggers if invoked
- [ ] Add simulation tests in `testing/src/upgrade.rs` simulating a failed migration and verifying automatic rollback

## Files to look at

- `contracts/upgradeability/src/lib.rs`
- `testing/src/upgrade.rs`
- `docs/MIGRATION_SAFETY.md`

## Acceptance criteria

- Upgrades automatically execute post-migration validation checks
- Any invariant violation during migration triggers an atomic rollback to the prior WASM hash
- Failed migrations cannot permanently trap contract funds

---
**Skills:** Rust, Soroban Bytecode Management, Formal Verification  
**Estimated effort:** 3–4 days

issues.title: access-control: Implement time-bounded role grants with automated timestamp expiration
issues.body:
In `contracts/access-control/src/lib.rs` (lines 75–85), `RoleMember(Symbol, Address)` stores only a boolean `bool`:

```rust
RoleMember(Symbol, Address),
```

Once granted, a role remains active indefinitely until an admin manually calls `revoke_role`.

## Why this matters

In humanitarian aid response, temporary personnel (e.g. disaster field workers, temporary auditors, relief contractors) only require access for a specific operational window (e.g. 14 days). Relying on manual revocation creates permission drift and leaves lingering administrative access on dormant accounts.

## Tasks

- [ ] Update `RoleMember` value to store `RoleGrant { active: bool, expires_at: Option<u64> }`
- [ ] Implement `grant_role_timed(env: Env, caller: Address, role: Symbol, account: Address, duration_seconds: u64) -> Result<(), Error>`
- [ ] In `has_role`, check if `expires_at.is_some() && env.ledger().timestamp() > expires_at`; if expired, treat as inactive
- [ ] Add query `get_role_expiration(env: Env, role: Symbol, account: Address) -> Option<u64>`
- [ ] Add unit tests in `contracts/access-control/src/lib.rs` verifying that time-bounded roles automatically expire without requiring revocation

## Files to look at

- `contracts/access-control/src/lib.rs`
- `docs/ACCESS_CONTROL.md`

## Acceptance criteria

- Admins can grant roles with an explicit expiration timestamp
- `has_role` returns `false` automatically once the timestamp passes
- Permanent role grants remain supported with `expires_at: None`

---
**Skills:** Rust, Access Control Systems  
**Estimated effort:** 1 day

issues.title: testing: Add cross-contract state fuzzing harness for concurrent aid, treasury, and referral execution
issues.body:
In `testing/src/`, individual contract mock suites and unit tests exist, but there is no integrated stateful fuzzing harness that exercises the full Trellis lifecycle under concurrent multi-user transactions: aid creation -> donation -> treasury reserve rebalancing -> aid claim -> referral commission accrual -> treasury reward distribution.

## Why this matters

Subtle race conditions, rounding dust accumulation, and cross-contract auth failures only emerge when multiple contracts interact concurrently under pseudo-randomized operation sequences. Without stateful fuzzing, cross-contract economic vulnerabilities remain undiscovered until deployed on mainnet.

## Tasks

- [ ] Build a stateful multi-contract fuzzing actor in `testing/src/fuzzing.rs` using `proptest`
- [ ] Generate randomized sequences of: `create_aid`, `deposit_treasury`, `register_referral`, `claim_aid`, `distribute_reward`, `rebalance`
- [ ] Validate global conservation invariant after every action: `Treasury Reserves + Escrowed Aid == Total Minted Tokens`
- [ ] Verify referral commission totals never exceed configured tier basis points
- [ ] Integrate harness into weekly CI schedule (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`)

## Files to look at

- `testing/src/fuzzing.rs`
- `testing/src/sandbox.rs`
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml`

## Acceptance criteria

- Stateful fuzzer executes 1,000+ random operation sequences per test run
- Strict conservation invariants are validated across all contract boundaries
- Fuzzer automatically discovers and reports any unexpected panics or invariant violations

---
**Skills:** Rust, Property-based Testing, DeFi Security  
**Estimated effort:** 2–3 days

issues.title: ci: Implement automated Soroban transaction CPU and memory footprint profiling in pull request CI
issues.body:
In `.github/workflows/ci.yml`, the `wasm-size-budget` job measures compiled WASM file size against size thresholds. However, there is no CI check that profiles transaction execution CPU instructions, RAM consumption, and storage ledger footprint across contract operations.

## Why this matters

A PR that introduces an accidental $O(N)$ vector traversal or unbounded map lookup will pass WASM size checks and cargo tests while drastically increasing transaction fees and pushing contracts towards Soroban execution budget limits.

## Tasks

- [ ] Create a benchmark profiling script (e.g. `scripts/profile-budget.sh` or Rust benchmark harness in `testing/`) using Soroban SDK's `env.budget()`
- [ ] Profile key operations: `AidContract::create_aid`, `AidContract::claim_aid`, `TreasuryContract::withdraw`, `ReferralContract::register`, `RebalancerContract::rebalance`
- [ ] Add a GitHub Actions CI job `profile-budget` that runs on PRs and compares CPU/RAM footprint against baseline metrics on `main`
- [ ] Post an automated comment or fail the check if CPU instructions or footprint increase by more than a configurable threshold (e.g. 10%)
- [ ] Document benchmark baseline thresholds in `docs/OBSERVABILITY.md`

## Files to look at

- `.github/workflows/ci.yml`
- `contracts/treasury-contract/src/budget_test.rs`
- `docs/OBSERVABILITY.md`

## Acceptance criteria

- CI automatically profiles CPU and memory consumption on every PR
- Regression warnings highlight unexpected increases in computational complexity
- Maintainers gain clear visibility into gas and fee implications of code changes

---
**Skills:** GitHub Actions, CI/CD, Soroban Profiling  
**Estimated effort:** 2 days

issues.title: docs: Add formal protocol verification invariant specifications and security threat model
issues.body:
The `docs/` directory contains operational runbooks, lifecycle state machine charts, and migration safety guides. However, it lacks a formal mathematical specification of core protocol invariants and an adversarial security threat model.

## Why this matters

External auditors, institutional NGO partners, and security researchers need an authoritative reference defining exact ledger invariants (e.g. solvency, non-reentrancy, access hierarchy boundaries) and an analysis of protocol resilience against known vectors (economic oracle manipulation, front-running, griefing, referral cycle Sybils).

  - Token conservation across Treasury, Aid, and Escrow
  - Referral graph acyclicity and non-dilution bounds
  - Oracle median deviation thresholds and staleness bounds
  - Access control privilege hierarchy and admin non-revocability
- [ ] Create `docs/THREAT_MODEL.md` documenting:
  - Trust assumptions (Admin keys, Oracle submitters, Stellar validators)
  - Adversarial attack vectors and protocol mitigation mechanisms
  - Emergency response and pause runbooks
- [ ] Link these documents in `README.md` and `docs/AUDIT.md`

## Files to look at

- `docs/THREAT_MODEL.md`
- `docs/AUDIT.md`
- `README.md`

## Acceptance criteria

- Complete security threat model document covering trust assumptions and mitigation strategies
